questions.q: What are the three possible states of a Promise?
options: loading, success, error
pending, fulfilled, rejected
waiting, done, failed
open, resolved, closed
questions.explain: A Promise starts pending, then settles permanently into either fulfilled (success) or rejected (failure).

questions.q: Once a Promise has settled (fulfilled or rejected), what happens if its resolve or reject function is called again?
options: It switches to the other state
Nothing — a settled promise can never change state again
It throws a runtime error
It restarts as pending
questions.explain: A promise can only settle once; calling resolve or reject again after it has already settled has no effect.

questions.q: In a .then().catch().finally() chain, when does the .finally() callback run?
options: Only if the promise is fulfilled
Only if the promise is rejected
Only if neither .then() nor .catch() was called
Always, regardless of whether the promise fulfilled or rejected
questions.explain: .finally() runs no matter the outcome, which is why it's commonly used for cleanup work like closing a connection or hiding a loading spinner.

questions.q: Why does chaining getUser(id).then(user => getBalance(user.address)).then(balance => getTransactions(balance.account)) avoid the nesting problem callbacks had?
options: Because .then() runs synchronously
Because each .then() returns a new promise, so dependent steps chain in a flat line instead of nesting inside each other
Because promises don't support error handling
Because getBalance and getTransactions aren't actually asynchronous
questions.explain: Each .then() call returns a new promise, letting you chain the next .then() off of it at the same indentation level rather than nesting deeper.

questions.q: What does Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]) do if p2 rejects while p1 and p3 are still pending?
options: It waits for p1 and p3 before rejecting
It ignores the rejection and returns whatever did resolve
It rejects immediately with p2's reason, without waiting for p1 or p3
It retries p2 automatically
questions.explain: Promise.all rejects as soon as any one of its promises rejects, regardless of the state of the others.
